### 2.1.3 Individual consultants/ service providers
Individual consultants or service providers are recruited for similar activities as Consultancy/ Service providing firms when a full team is not considered necessary. They may be independent experts not permanently associated with any particular firm, or they may be employees of a firm recruited on an individual basis. They may also be employees of an agency, institution, or university. They are normally recruited for project implementation supervision, training, provision of specific expert advice on a highly technical subject, policy guidance, special studies, compliance supervision, or implementation monitoring. Individual consultants/ service providers are not normally recruited for project preparation unless the proposed project is simple and, generally, a repeat of an already established and successful project. If more than three experts are required, then the assignment should normally be undertaken by a team from a firm. As with firms, individual consultants/ service providers are classed as either international or national, depending on their level of expertise and their international experience and exposure.

### 2.1.4 Specialized Agencies and Institutions
Specialized agencies or institutions (including Government/ Semi-Government agencies, universities and professional institutions) may also from time to time be recruited to provide Consultancy/ other services. These services may be provided by individuals (as discussed above) or by teams. Nonetheless, there are at times distinct advantages to using such agencies. Experts and teams from such agencies and institutions may undertake a variety of roles across the whole field of possible Consultancy and other services. These may range from project preparation through project supervision and policy advice to project benefit monitoring and evaluation.

### 2.1.5 Non-governmental Organizations (NGO)
There may be distinct advantage in use of Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in Projects which emphasize experience in community participation and in-depth local knowledge - for example, Projects related to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

### 2.1.6 Retired Government Servant
The consulting services do not include direct engagement of retired Government servants. They should not be engaged against regular vacant posts as consultant under this rule. Retired Government servants can be engaged only for the specific task and for specific duration as consultant. They should be assigned clear output related goals.

question_text: What minimum percentage threshold must the price variation formula stipulate for an upward price adjustment to be admissible?
answer: - Verify that the price variation clause specifies a minimum percentage threshold for admissible upward price adjustments (e.g., not less than 2 % of the contract price); any upward variation below this threshold shall not be payable to the supplier. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 111)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint the requirement for when an upward price adjustment is allowed. The question is asking for the minimum percentage that must be set in the price‑variation formula before any upward adjustment can be made.  

The relevant provision addresses the price variation formula needing to stipulate a minimum percentage of variation; only when the calculated change exceeds that threshold does the adjustment become payable. The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals illustrate this: if the resulting increase is lower than, say, two per cent of the contract price, no price adjustment will be made in favour of the supplier.  

That example makes it clear that the intended threshold is two percent—any increase below that amount is considered too small to warrant an adjustment, so the formula must specify at least that level.  

Therefore, to satisfy the requirement for an admissible upward price adjustment, the clause must state that the price variation will only be allowed if it equals or exceeds two percent of the contract price; variations below that figure are not payable to the supplier.  

Putting it together, the minimum percentage threshold the price variation formula must stipulate for an upward price adjustment to be admissible is two percent of the contract price.

question_text: What right does the procuring entity retain even after a consignment has been cleared by a third‑party inspection authority
answer: - Verify that the procuring entity retains the explicit right to reject a consignment even when the consignment has been cleared by a third‑party inspection authority. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 159)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know which authority or privilege the procuring entity keeps hold of even after an outside inspection body has given the consignment a clean bill of health.  

Next, I consider what it means for a third‑party inspection to clear a shipment. Their role is to assess conformity against the technical specifications, but their verdict is not necessarily final in the procurement process; the contract usually reserves certain powers for the buyer.  

Then I think about the typical safeguards built into procurement agreements. Even when an external expert says the goods are okay, the procuring entity often retains a veto to protect its own interests—especially if later testing, performance issues, or contractual non‑compliance surface.  

Looking at the specific provision that governs this situation, it states clearly that the procuring entity “retains the right to reject the consignment, even if it is cleared by third‑party inspection authorities.” This wording makes it explicit that the inspection outcome does not override the buyer’s authority to refuse acceptance.  

Finally, synthesizing these points, the right that remains with the procuring entity after a third‑party clearance is precisely the right to reject the consignment if it deems the goods unsatisfactory or non‑conforming. This matches the answer: the procuring entity retains the explicit right to reject a consignment even when it has been cleared by a third‑party inspection authority.

#### iii) **Joint Inspection on Complaint**
In case a written complaint is received from the supplier disputing the rejection of goods by the Procuring Entity's inspecting officer, it should be jointly investigated by a team consisting of an authorised representative of the Procuring Entity, a senior representative of the inspecting agency who is conversant with the goods and an authorised representative of the supplier.

Among those threats, landslides are explicitly mentioned as one of the hazards for which the Atlas has prepared additional digitized maps.

This combination—maps showing where landslides have occurred and the climatic context of rainfall—gives a basis for judging how prone a particular location might be to future landslide events.  
Therefore, when carrying out site evaluation, the Atlas can be consulted to obtain both the spatial landslide data and the rainfall‑linked incidence records, enabling a risk assessment for landslides.  
Putting these points together, the Atlas supplies digitized landslide maps and includes data on landslide incidences together with the annual rainfall normal for the area, which can be used to assess landslide risk when evaluating a site.

question_text: When is adequate fund required for an outline agreement (ARC)?
answer: - Adequate fund is required for an outline agreement (ARC) only at the time of issuing the Release Order. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 71)
cot:
I need to figure out when an outline agreement, or ARC, actually requires that adequate funds be in place.  
First, I think about the usual procurement flow: you estimate costs, get budget approval, create a purchase requisition and order, and then expenses are posted when the service entry sheet is accepted.  
But the question is specifically about ARCs, so I look for any special rule that might override the standard process.  
In the section dealing with approvals and budgeting, there’s a note that says for outline agreements the funding requirement is tied to a later step—only when the release order is issued.  
That means the earlier stages, like the PR or PO, don’t demand that the money already be earmarked; the commitment is made later, at the point the release order is generated.  
Putting those pieces together, the adequate fund for an ARC is needed precisely at the moment the release order is issued, not before.  
Hence, the answer is that adequate fund is required for an outline agreement (ARC) only at the time of issuing the Release Order.

### 9.9.2 **Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and seeking Approval.**
Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked. The cost estimate shall be based on the Procuring Entity's assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment: managerial and staff time and physical inputs (for example, materials, consumables, tools and machines). Costs shall be divided into three broad categories:

- i) Remunerations for Personnel deployed;
- ii) Reimbursable: (Travel, logistics, Consumable, Material, Tools, Hiring of third party services etc.);
- iii) Administrative and Miscellaneous (Mobilisation, demobilisation, Temporary Structures, Administrative expenses, office and IT equipment, contingencies, financing costs, Costs for hiring/ depreciation/ financing of machinery and equipment etc).

The Activity Schedule shall be compatible with the available budget. The most important step is to determine whether all tasks required to achieve the desired output have been included. The next step is to determine whether adequate budget has been allocated to implement the assignment as designed. Procurement should be initiated only after such approvals and budgetary provisions.

question_text: What responsibility does the CA have when accepting a tender, ordering negotiations, or calling for a re‑tender
answer: - The CA shall exercise due diligence when accepting a tender, ordering negotiations, or calling for a re‑tender. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 128)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants to know what the Contracting Authority (CA) must do when it is faced with accepting a tender, deciding to order negotiations, or issuing a call for a re‑tender.  

Next, I look at the situation surrounding each of those actions. The Procurement of Goods Manual makes clear that negotiations are not the norm; they should be rare, limited to the lowest acceptable bidder, and only undertaken when exceptional circumstances exist, with convincing reasons recorded. Likewise, the choice between negotiating, re‑tendering, or simply accepting a tender must be made by the procuring department or the TEC, and the authority recommending any deviation must justify it.  

Seeing these points together, I notice a common theme: whenever the CA steps away from the standard tender‑acceptance path—whether to negotiate or to call for a fresh tender—it must do so with careful scrutiny, ensuring that any exception is warranted and properly documented.  

The Procurement of Goods Manual explicitly ties this idea together by stating that the CA should exercise due diligence while accepting a tender, ordering negotiations, or calling for a re‑tender. This captures the need for thorough, prudent judgment in each of those scenarios.  

Putting it all together, the responsibility that falls on the CA in those moments is to act with due diligence, making sure every decision is well‑considered, justified, and in line with proper procurement practice.

question_text: Which statement records the allocation or use of materials under the contract
answer: The material appropriation statement records the allocation or use of materials under the contract (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 108).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really after: it wants to know which specific statement, among those mentioned in the contract documentation, captures how materials are allocated or used under the contract.  

The Procurement of Works Manual enumerates the supporting documents that must accompany a contract‑closing proposal. Each bullet describes a different kind of statement or certificate.  

Among those bullets, one stands out: “A material appropriation statement.” The phrase “material appropriation” directly evokes the idea of assigning or using materials—essentially recording what materials have been allocated to the work and how they have been consumed.  

The other items—excess‑saving statement, time‑extension statement, work‑completion certificate, recoveries/deductions statement, no‑claim certificate, labour liability certificate, etc.—deal with financial, temporal, or liability aspects, not with the physical allocation of materials.  

Therefore, the only document that serves the purpose of recording the allocation or use of materials is the material appropriation statement.  

Putting it together, the answer is that the material appropriation statement records the allocation or use of materials under the contract.

From this I infer that the bulk of the bid document—such as the Notice Inviting Tenders, the Instructions to Bidders themselves, the General Conditions of Contract, the Technical Specifications, the Schedule of Rates, the Forms of Bid, the Bill of Quantities, and the standard formats—are to be copied unchanged from the SBD, while project‑specific details belong only in those two variable sections.

question_text: What is considered the essence of the contract for the purchaser in a supply contract
answer: Delivery of goods is the essence of the contract for the purchaser in a supply contract. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 107)
cot:
First, I need to unpack what “essence of the contract” really means—it’s the fundamental obligation that defines the purpose of the agreement for each party.  
In a supply contract there are two sides: the purchaser, who acquires the goods, and the supplier, who provides them.  
Thinking about what each side primarily wants helps clarify their core obligations; the purchaser’s main goal is to obtain the goods in the right quantity, quality and time, whereas the supplier’s main goal is to receive payment for those goods.  
Since the purchaser’s satisfaction hinges on actually getting the goods delivered as promised, the delivery of goods becomes the central, defining duty for them in the contract.  
Therefore, the essence of the contract for the purchaser in a supply contract is the delivery of goods.

question_text: When is FORMAT-2C required to be submitted?
answer:
- FORMAT‑2C must be submitted with the unpriced bid whenever the tender is a **multiple‑item, splitable tender** (i.e., the procurement consists of several distinct items that may be awarded separately).  
- It provides an item‑wise declaration of the minimum local content to demonstrate compliance with the PP‑LC policy.  
- Including FORMAT‑2C supports transparency, ensures value for money, and aligns procurement practices with corporate risk‑management and strategic objectives.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 255)
cot:
I need to figure out exactly when the bidder has to include FORMAT‑2C with their submission. The question is straightforward: it’s asking for the trigger condition that makes this form mandatory. 

First, I recall that FORMAT‑2C is titled “Declaration of Minimum Local Content (item wise)” and the note attached to it says it’s applicable for a “Multiple Item Splitable Tender.” That phrasing suggests the form is only relevant when the procurement is broken down into several distinct items that could be awarded separately. If the tender were for a single, indivisible item, there would be no need to declare local content on an item‑by‑item basis; a single overall declaration would suffice.

Next, I think about where this form fits in the bid package. The reference shows it alongside other unpriced‑bid documents like FORMAT‑2B, and it explicitly states that it must be uploaded along with the unpriced bid. The unpriced bid contains all technical and compliance information before the price envelope is opened, so any declaration that proves eligibility—such as meeting the local‑content thresholds—has to be there at that stage. Therefore, the timing is clear: the form travels with the unpriced bid, not with the price bid.

Now, why is the item‑wise detail important? The PP‑LC policy sets different minimum local‑content percentages for Class‑I and Class‑II suppliers. When a tender contains multiple items, each item might have a different local‑content composition, and the buyer needs to verify that every single item meets the required threshold before awarding any part of the contract. FORMAT‑2C provides that granular proof, line by line, for each item in the splitable tender.

Putting those pieces together, the form serves a broader procurement purpose: it makes the local‑content compliance transparent, helps the buyer achieve value for money by ensuring that only eligible items move forward, and aligns the process with the organization’s risk‑management and strategic objectives of promoting local sourcing.

So, synthesizing the above, FORMAT‑2C must be submitted with the unpriced bid whenever the tender is a multiple‑item, splitable tender—i.e., when the procurement consists of several distinct items that may be awarded separately. This requirement ensures an item‑wise declaration of minimum local content, supports transparency, secures value for money, and fits within the corporate risk‑management and strategic framework.

question_text: How may the Earnest Money Deposit of a successful bidder be treated under the NRL manual if it falls short of the required Initial Security Deposit?
answer: The Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of a successful bidder that is insufficient to meet the required Initial Security Deposit (ISD) can be addressed in two ways under the NRL manual. First, the EMD may be converted to the ISD by the bidder making good the shortfall amount between the EMD and the ISD stipulated for the contract. Second, the bidder has the option to withdraw the EMD and, instead, submit a separate Bank Guarantee (BG) in lieu of the ISD/SD, prepared according to the proforma in Annexure 17. The BG must remain valid for three months beyond the later of contract completion or the end of the defect liability period. When a BG is accepted, the sponsoring function must ensure that the BG conforms to the prescribed proforma, that online systems are available for its monitoring and handling, that timely renewal is effected when required, and that prompt action is taken to realize the EMD from the bank upon any contractor breach. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 64)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know how the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of a bidder who wins the contract should be handled when that deposit does not reach the amount required for the Initial Security Deposit (ISD).  

Under the NRL manual, the key point is that on award of contract the EMD can either be turned into the ISD or be taken back and replaced by another form of security.  

If the EMD is to become the ISD, the bidder must cover any difference between what they have already deposited and what the ISD calls for; in other words, they make good the shortfall so that the total equals the required ISD.  

Alternatively, the bidder may choose to withdraw the EMD entirely and instead provide a Bank Guarantee that stands in lieu of the ISD/SD. The guarantee has to follow the proforma given in Annexure 17 and stay valid for three months beyond the later of contract completion or the end of the defect liability period.  

When a Bank Guarantee is accepted, the sponsoring function has to verify that the guarantee matches the prescribed format, set up online tracking for it, renew it promptly when needed, and be ready to call on the guarantee if the contractor breaches any term of the tender or contract.  

Putting these two pathways together, the EMD of a successful bidder that falls short of the ISD can either be supplemented to reach the ISD amount or be withdrawn and replaced by a compliant Bank Guarantee with the stated safeguards. This matches the description of the treatment under the NRL manual.

question_text: Who must release the Purchase Requisition after it is created by the user department
answer: The Purchase Requisition must be released by the Competent Authority after it is created by the user department. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 45)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: after a user department creates a Purchase Requisition, which role or authority is responsible for giving it the go‑ahead to move forward in the procurement process.  

Next, I recall the typical flow of a procurement initiation: the user department identifies a need, drafts the requisition with all required details, and then it must be cleared before any further action such as sourcing or issuing a purchase order can take place.  

Thinking about the approval step, the Procurement of Goods Manual describes that the user department creates the PR through the Aarohan system and then gets it “released by the Competent Authority” after confirming that there is an actual requirement for the goods. This phrasing makes it clear that the release is not done by the user department itself, nor by a commercial or technical team, but by a designated authority that has the competence to sanction the requisition.  

I also note that while the Commercial Department may review a PR and send it back for clarification, the act of releasing it—i.e., authorizing it to proceed—is still attributed to the Competent Authority; the Commercial Department’s role is advisory, not decisive.  

Putting these observations together, the only entity that the Procurement of Goods Manual assigns the responsibility of releasing the PR after its creation is the Competent Authority. Therefore, the answer must be that the Purchase Requisition must be released by the Competent Authority after it is created by the user department.

question_text: How can initial essential spares be addressed in capital goods procurement
answer:
Effective procurement of capital goods integrates initial essential spares to safeguard operational continuity and protect the organization’s investment.  

- Embed contractual clauses that obligate the supplier to deliver essential initial spares sufficient for two years of maintenance together with the equipment. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 140)  
- Explicitly capture the cost of these spares in the equipment’s description, specification and contract conditions, and evaluate it as part of the total present value of the acquisition (e.g., using DCF analysis for related AMCs). (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 140‑141)  
- Treat the spares provision as an investment decision that supports value‑for‑money, reduces downtime risk and aligns with strategic goals of transparency and sustained asset performance. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 140‑141)
cot:
I start by asking what the real problem is when we acquire a piece of capital equipment: we need it to stay operational from day one, otherwise any delay caused by a missing part can erase the benefits of the investment.  

Looking at how capital goods are procured, I notice that the process already treats the purchase as more than just handing over a machine—it bundles installation, commissioning, training, warranty, after‑sales service and, importantly, the provision of spares.  

That observation leads me to think that the contract can simply be extended to oblige the supplier to deliver a specific set of essential spares that will be sufficient for two years of routine maintenance, and that this obligation should be written into the agreement alongside the warranty period and service‑level penalties.  

Next, I consider the financial side: if those spares are not priced into the deal, the true cost of acquisition is hidden. So the spares’ cost must be made explicit in the equipment’s description and specification, and it should be added to the total price that is evaluated— for instance, by incorporating it into the present value calculation of any associated annual maintenance contracts using a discounted cash flow approach.  

Finally, I see that treating the spares requirement as part of the investment decision itself makes sense: it safeguards continuous operation, protects the organization’s capital outlay, and contributes to overall value‑for‑money by minimizing downtime risk and supporting long‑term asset performance.  

Putting these thoughts together, the way to address initial essential spares in capital goods procurement is to embed contractual clauses for their delivery, capture their cost in the specification and evaluate it as part of the total present value of the acquisition, and view the whole package as an investment that ensures operational continuity and protects the organization’s investment.

question_text: How should provisions be made for a scheme that includes revenue component, capital expenditure, and loan content, etc., requiring separate heads of account?
answer: For a scheme that includes revenue components, capital expenditure, and loan content, provisions should be made separately under the respective heads of account for each element. However, the scheme must be regarded as an integrated whole when seeking sanction; the competent authority must approve it based on the total cost, and the scheme cannot be split into parts to obtain approval from a lower authority. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 14)
cot:
I need to figure out how to handle provisions when a scheme mixes revenue items, capital spending and loan elements, especially since each of those items has to be shown under its own head of account. First, I think about why the heads have to be separate – revenue costs are treated differently from capital outlays and from borrowed funds, so the accounting rules demand that each type be recorded under its own heading to keep the financial statements clear and compliant. That tells me that when I set aside money for the scheme, I should allocate the revenue part to the revenue head, the capital part to the capital head and the loan portion to the loan head, making sure each element is provisioned in its appropriate account.

Next, I consider the approval process. Even though the money is kept in separate accounts, the scheme itself is a single undertaking; its success depends on all the pieces working together. Therefore, the authority that gives the go‑ahead has to look at the total cost of the whole scheme, not just the sum of the parts taken individually. This means I cannot seek sanction for each component separately in order to slip under a lower authority’s limit; the rule is clear that splitting a scheme to avoid higher‑level approval is not allowed.

Putting those thoughts together, I see that the correct approach is to make provisions for each element under its respective head of account, but to treat the scheme as an integrated whole when requesting sanction. The competent authority must approve the scheme based on the aggregate cost, and any attempt to divide it up to obtain approval from a lower authority would be impermissible. That matches the required answer: separate heads for revenue, capital and loan, with an overall sanction based on total cost and no splitting to evade higher authority approval.

- i) No new works should be sanctioned without
  - i) Careful assessment of the assets or facilities already available and time and cost required to complete the new works.
  - ii) A concept plan/ preliminary drawing have been approved by the Authority competent to accord sanction. While designing projects to the extent possible, principles of Life Cycle Costing may also be considered;
- ii) As budgetary resources are limited and granted on annual basis, adequate provisions should be ensured for works and services already in progress before new works are undertaken.
- iii) No project or work will be split up to bring it within the sanctioning powers of a lower authority.
- iv) For purpose of approval and sanctions, a group of works which forms one project, shall be considered as one work. The approval or sanction of the higher authority for such a project which consists of such a group of work should not be circumvented by resorting to approval of individual works using the powers of approval or sanction of a lower authority. If the component parts of a project are mutually independent of each other and are not dependent on the execution of one or more such component parts, each such part should be treated as a separate project. In case the functioning of a project is dependent on the execution of one or more other projects, the entire group of such projects should be taken as a single scheme/ project and provision made accordingly. If however, a scheme consists of revenue component, capital expenditure and loan content, etc. the provision for which is required to be exhibited separately under respective Heads of Account, there is no objection to the provision being made in the relevant Heads of Account;

but the authorities concerned should ensure that the sanction of the Competent Authority is obtained for the integrated scheme as a whole depending on the total cost of the scheme. It will not be permissible in such cases to split up a scheme treating each part as a scheme in order to avoid the sanction of a higher authority.
